keyLines.note: The world is muddy and unclear, so that a cicada's wing counts as heavy and a thousand-weight counts as light.

keyLines.line: 黃鐘毀棄，瓦釜雷鳴；讒人高張，賢士無名
keyLines.en: The Yellow Bell is smashed and cast aside, while clay pots thunder; slanderers are exalted, and worthy men have no name.
keyLines.note: The noble Yellow Bell is destroyed while the lowly clay pot is loud; slanderers rise and worthy men go unknown.

keyLines.line: 夫尺有所短，寸有所長
keyLines.en: A foot is short in some places, an inch is long in others.
keyLines.note: A foot has its shortcomings and an inch its strengths; everything has its own length and shortness.

keyLines.line: 用君之心，行君之意，龜策誠不能知事
keyLines.en: Use your own heart and carry out your own intention; the tortoise and the stalks truly cannot know this matter.
keyLines.note: Follow your own mind; the tortoise shell and stalks cannot actually decide this for you.

glossary.note: The official in charge of divination.

glossary.en: Zheng Zhanyin - the diviner Zheng Zhanyin
glossary.note: A name for the Grand Diviner; some think he is an invented figure.

glossary.en: duan ce fu gui - to straighten the stalks and brush the tortoise shell
glossary.note: To set the yarrow stalks straight and wipe dust from the tortoise shell, in preparation to divine. Ce are the stalks; gui is the shell.

glossary.en: kun kun kuan kuan - sincere and earnest
glossary.note: Honest and devoted.

glossary.en: song wang lao lai - to see off and welcome
glossary.note: To greet and send off visitors, meaning social flattery and entertaining.

glossary.en: zu zi li si, wo yi ru er - fawning and cringing
glossary.note: Describes grovelling and ingratiating behaviour.

glossary.en: tu ti gu ji - smooth and slippery
glossary.note: Rounded off, going along with the fashion, adapting to everything.

glossary.en: Huang Zhong hui qi, wa fu lei ming - the Yellow Bell is smashed, the clay pot thunders
glossary.note: The Yellow Bell is a noble musical instrument and the clay pot a lowly cooking vessel; the saying means worthy men are cast aside while petty men prosper.

buju.background: The 'Bu Ju' (Divination) and 'Yu Fu' (The Fisherman) are usually credited to Qu Yuan, but the text speaks of 'Qu Yuan' in the third person, and many scholars think they were written later from his story and thought, or are accounts by people of Chu. The string of parallel questions influenced the elaborate style of later fu. 'An inch has its strengths and a foot its shortfalls' is a saying still used today.

yufu.summary: A Chuci piece written as a dialogue between Qu Yuan and a fisherman. Qu Yuan says the whole world is muddy and he alone is clear, everyone is drunk and he alone is sober; the fisherman urges him to go with the times and not be so unbending. Qu Yuan answers that he would rather die than let his clean body gather the dust of the world, and the fisherman smiles and leaves singing the Canglang song. The two attitudes to life are set against each other, with strong tension.
yufu.translation:
After Qu Yuan was exiled, he wandered by the river pools, walking and chanting on the marsh bank, his face worn and his body wasted. A fisherman saw him and asked: "Are you not the Grand Master of the Three Clans? What has brought you to this?"
Qu Yuan said: "The whole world is muddy and I alone am clear; everyone is drunk and I alone am sober. That is why I was exiled."
The fisherman said: "The sage does not cling to things, but can move with the world. If the whole world is muddy, why not stir the mud and raise the waves? If everyone is drunk, why not eat the dregs and sip the thin wine? Why brood so deeply and hold yourself so high that you bring exile on yourself?"
Qu Yuan said: "I have heard that one who has just washed his hair must flick his cap, and one who has just bathed must shake out his clothes. How can I let a body so clear take in the filth of things? I would rather throw myself into the Xiang and be buried in the bellies of river fish than let my gleaming white be covered in the dust of the world."
The fisherman smiled, beat the oar and left, singing: "When the water of Canglang is clear, I can wash my cap strings in it; when the water of Canglang is muddy, I can wash my feet in it." Then he went off and said no more to him.

keyLines.line: 舉世皆濁我獨清，眾人皆醉我獨醒
keyLines.en: The whole world is muddy and I alone am clear; everyone is drunk and I alone am sober.
keyLines.note: The whole world is murky and only he is pure; everyone is muddled with drink and only he is awake.

keyLines.line: 聖人不凝滯於物，而能與世推移
keyLines.en: The sage does not cling to things, but can move with the world.
keyLines.note: A sage is not stuck on things and can change with the times; this is the fisherman's way of living.

keyLines.line: 新沐者必彈冠，新浴者必振衣
keyLines.en: One who has just washed his hair must flick his cap, and one who has just bathed must shake out his clothes.
keyLines.note: A person who has just washed his hair brushes his cap, and one who has bathed shakes out his clothes: neither wants a clean body to pick up dust.

keyLines.line: 寧赴湘流，葬於江魚之腹中
keyLines.en: I would rather throw myself into the Xiang and be buried in the bellies of river fish.
keyLines.note: He would rather drown in the Xiang and feed the fish than go along with the filth.

keyLines.line: 滄浪之水清兮，可以濯吾纓；滄浪之水濁兮，可以濯吾足
keyLines.en: When the water of Canglang is clear, I can wash my cap strings in it; when the water of Canglang is muddy, I can wash my feet in it.
keyLines.note: If the water is clear one washes the cap strings; if muddy, the feet. It means adapting to circumstances and being content wherever one is.

glossary.en: San Lu dafu - Grand Master of the Three Clans
glossary.note: The post in Chu that oversaw the three royal clans of Qu, Jing and Zhao; Qu Yuan held it.

glossary.en: ning zhi - to cling, to be stuck
glossary.note: To be inflexible and unable to move on.

glossary.en: gu qi ni er yang qi bo - to stir the mud and raise the waves
glossary.note: To churn up mud and make waves, meaning to go with the flow.

glossary.en: bu qi zao er chuo qi li - to eat the dregs and sip the thin wine
glossary.note: To eat the lees and drink the weak wine, meaning to get drunk along with everyone else (li is thin wine).

glossary.en: cha cha, men men - spotless, murky
glossary.note: Cha cha is clean and pure; wen wen is dirty and dim.

glossary.en: gu yi - to beat the oar
glossary.note: To strike the oar against the boat, or to row.
A river name, in the lower Han, and also a general term for clear water.
The ribbon that ties a cap.

yufu.background: The 'Yu Fu' is also usually credited to Qu Yuan, but it is told in the third person like 'Bu Ju', and modern scholars mostly doubt that he wrote it. The fisherman became a lasting image of the recluse. The lines 「滄浪之水清兮，可以濯吾纓」 ("when the water of Canglang is clear, I can wash my cap strings in it") also appear in the 'Song of the Boy' recorded in the Mencius, showing the verse was an old folk song. Qu Yuan's reply stands for his refusal to go with the current.
